faq.q: What is the most common cause of postpartum endometritis?

faq.q: Why add metronidazole to the regimen?

faq.a: After 48 h of afebrile status, clinical improvement, and at least 5 days total therapy, provided no complications.

exam: A woman 2 days post‑cesarean presents with fever 38.5 °C, uterine tenderness, and foul lochia. What is your immediate management? — Start broad‑spectrum IV antibiotics (ampicillin + gentamicin + metronidazole) and obtain blood cultures.

How does WHO sepsis staging guide treatment in postpartum infection? — Progression from SIRS to septic shock dictates escalation from oral/IV antibiotics to aggressive fluid resuscitation and vasopressors.
A postpartum patient has fever but a normal WBC. Does this rule out infection? — No; WBC can be normal; rely on clinical signs and other investigations.
Why is clindamycin avoided in a severely anemic postpartum woman? — It can cause bone‑marrow suppression, worsening anemia.

Differentiate postpartum endometritis from pyelonephritis based on bedside findings. — Endometritis: uterine tenderness, foul lochia; pyelonephritis: flank pain, costovertebral angle tenderness, dysuria.

If ampicillin is unavailable, which alternative provides similar coverage in low‑resource settings? — Use a combination of ceftriaxone (if available) plus metronidazole; otherwise, high‑dose gentamicin with metronidazole.
What are the red‑flag signs indicating septic shock in a postpartum patient? — Hypotension (SBP <90 mmHg), lactate >2 mmol/L, altered mental status, oliguria.
Explain why retained placental tissue predisposes to postpartum infection. — It serves as a nidus for bacterial growth, prolonging inflammation and providing a medium for anaerobes.
ai.title: Postpartum Infections
ai.subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
ai.summary: Postpartum infections are bacterial or polymicrobial infections occurring within 6 weeks after delivery. Prompt recognition, appropriate investigations and targeted therapy are essential, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Incidence higher in low‑resource hospitals (up to 10 %).
Common pathogens: Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes, anaerobes, E. coli, Group B Strep, and polymicrobial flora.
sections.p: Infection after childbirth can involve the uterus, genital tract, urinary system, or surgical wound. Mortality is highest in the first 48 hours and in women with HIV, anemia, or prolonged labor.

b: Fever ≥38 °C after the first 24 h postpartum is abnormal.
Uterine fundal tenderness or foul‑smelling lochia suggests endometritis.
Hypotension with lactate >2 mmol/L indicates septic shock.
sections.p: Diagnosis relies on clinical criteria (fever, uterine tenderness, foul lochia) plus simple bedside tests. Severity is staged by the WHO sepsis criteria (SIRS → sepsis → severe sepsis → septic shock).

b: Risk factors: prolonged rupture of membranes >18 h, cesarean delivery, retained placental tissue, anemia, HIV, malaria, malnutrition.
Complications: pelvic abscess, peritonitis, septic thrombophlebitis, disseminated intravascular coagulation.
sections.p: Early identification prevents progression to severe sepsis, organ failure, and death. In low‑resource settings, limited labs mean reliance on bedside assessment and empiric therapy.

t.b: Is there a persistent fever? – Persistent ≥38 °C after 24 h suggests infection.
Leukocytosis or left shift? – WBC >12 000 /µL or neutrophils >80 % supports infection; normal count does not rule out.
Is there a urinary infection? – Positive leukocyte esterase or nitrites indicates UTI, a common postpartum source.
Is the patient in shock? – Lactate >2 mmol/L suggests tissue hypoperfusion.
Is there retained tissue or abscess? – Fluid collection or echogenic material in the uterine cavity indicates retained products or abscess.

b: First‑line: ampicillin + gentamicin + metronidazole (covers Gram‑positive, Gram‑negative, anaerobes).
Avoid clindamycin in severe anemia due to risk of bone‑marrow suppression.
If clostridial infection suspected, add high‑dose penicillin.
If antibiotics unavailable, use the most accessible effective agent (e.g., ampicillin alone) and arrange transfer.
sections.p: Start broad‑spectrum antibiotics promptly, then narrow based on culture (if obtainable). Provide supportive care: fluids, oxygen, and monitor vitals.

b: Ask about duration of rupture of membranes and mode of delivery.
Examine uterine size, tenderness, and lochia character.
Check for flank pain and dysuria to rule out pyelonephritis.
sections.p: Examiners often test integration of history, risk factors, and sepsis staging. They may ask about immediate steps, drug choice rationale, and distinguishing endometritis from urinary infection.

b: Ignoring low‑grade fever in the first 24 h (often physiological).
Relying on a normal WBC to exclude infection.
Choosing a single‑drug regimen without anaerobic coverage.
sections.p: Mistaking normal postpartum lochia for infection, delaying antibiotics, and using narrow‑spectrum agents when polymicrobial flora is likely.

whenToSeekHelp: Fever >38 °C persisting >24 h, hypotension, altered mental status, oliguria, or rapidly worsening pain.
